claim: COMMD proteins are a conserved family of proteins with central roles in intracellular membrane trafficking and transcription.
source: The COMMD proteins are a conserved family of proteins with central roles in intracellular membrane trafficking and transcription.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a general characterization of COMMD proteins.

claim: COMMD proteins form oligomeric complexes with each other.
source: They form oligomeric complexes with each other and act as components of a larger assembly called the CCC complex, which is localized to endosomal compartments and mediates the transport of several transmembrane cargos.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known property of COMMD proteins.

claim: COMMD proteins act as components of the CCC complex.
source: They form oligomeric complexes with each other and act as components of a larger assembly called the CCC complex, which is localized to endosomal compartments and mediates the transport of several transmembrane cargos.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known property of COMMD proteins.

claim: The CCC complex is localized to endosomal compartments.
source: They form oligomeric complexes with each other and act as components of a larger assembly called the CCC complex, which is localized to endosomal compartments and mediates the transport of several transmembrane cargos.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known property of the CCC complex.

claim: The CCC complex mediates the transport of several transmembrane cargos.
source: They form oligomeric complexes with each other and act as components of a larger assembly called the CCC complex, which is localized to endosomal compartments and mediates the transport of several transmembrane cargos.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known property of the CCC complex.

claim: All COMMD proteins possess an α-helical N-terminal domain.
source: All COMMD proteins possess an α-helical N-terminal domain, and a highly conserved C-terminal domain that forms a tightly interlocked dimeric structure responsible for COMMD-COMMD interactions.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by structural data presented in the manuscript.

claim: All COMMD proteins possess a highly conserved C-terminal domain.
source: All COMMD proteins possess an α-helical N-terminal domain, and a highly conserved C-terminal domain that forms a tightly interlocked dimeric structure responsible for COMMD-COMMD interactions.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by structural and sequence data.

claim: The C-terminal COMM domain forms a tightly interlocked dimeric structure.
source: All COMMD proteins possess an α-helical N-terminal domain, and a highly conserved C-terminal domain that forms a tightly interlocked dimeric structure responsible for COMMD-COMMD interactions.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by the crystal structure of the Commd9 COMM domain.

claim: The C-terminal COMM domain is responsible for COMMD-COMMD interactions.
source: All COMMD proteins possess an α-helical N-terminal domain, and a highly conserved C-terminal domain that forms a tightly interlocked dimeric structure responsible for COMMD-COMMD interactions.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by biochemical and biophysical data.

claim: The COMM domains bind directly to components of CCC.
source: The COMM domains also bind directly to components of CCC and mediate non-specific membrane association.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by biochemical binding assays.

claim: The COMM domains mediate non-specific membrane association.
source: The COMM domains also bind directly to components of CCC and mediate non-specific membrane association.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by liposome binding assays.

claim: COMMD proteins function as obligatory dimers.
source: Overall these studies show that COMMD proteins function as obligatory dimers with conserved domain architectures.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by multiple lines of evidence including MALLS, crystal structures, and mutagenesis.

claim: COMMD proteins have conserved domain architectures.
source: Overall these studies show that COMMD proteins function as obligatory dimers with conserved domain architectures.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by structural and bioinformatics analyses.

claim: COMMD proteins are highly conserved in metazoans and unicellular protozoa.
source: The COMMD (Copper Metabolism Murr1 (Mouse U2af1-rs1 region 1) Domain) proteins are highly conserved in metazoans and unicellular protozoa (Burstein et al., 2005; Maine and Burstein, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: There are ten COMMD family members.
source: There are ten family members that play key roles in intracellular trafficking and in the regulation of transcription (Burstein et al., 2005; Maine and Burstein, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: COMMD family members play key roles in intracellular trafficking.
source: There are ten family members that play key roles in intracellular trafficking and in the regulation of transcription (Burstein et al., 2005; Maine and Burstein, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: COMMD family members play key roles in the regulation of transcription.
source: There are ten family members that play key roles in intracellular trafficking and in the regulation of transcription (Burstein et al., 2005; Maine and Burstein, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The COMM domain is a highly conserved C-terminal sequence of ~70–80 amino acids.
source: A hallmark of the COMMD family members is a highly conserved C-terminal sequence of ~70–80 amino acids called the COMM domain, which has no known structure.
evidence: This is a known characteristic of COMMD proteins from previous literature.

claim: The COMM domain had no known structure prior to this study.
source: A hallmark of the COMMD family members is a highly conserved C-terminal sequence of ~70–80 amino acids called the COMM domain, which has no known structure.
evidence: This establishes the novelty of the structural work presented in this manuscript.

claim: The N-terminal domain of COMMD proteins is more variable in sequence across the ten proteins.
source: The N-terminal domain of these proteins, which we refer to as the HN (helical N-terminal) domain, is more variable in sequence across the ten proteins, and is proposed to ascribe unique functions to the different family members (Burstein et al., 2005; Maine and Burstein, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and sequence analysis.

claim: The N-terminal domain is proposed to ascribe unique functions to the different COMMD family members.
source: The N-terminal domain of these proteins, which we refer to as the HN (helical N-terminal) domain, is more variable in sequence across the ten proteins, and is proposed to ascribe unique functions to the different family members (Burstein et al., 2005; Maine and Burstein, 2007).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous literature.

claim: All ten members of the COMMD family (Commd1-Commd10) are expressed broadly in many tissues in humans.
source: In humans, all ten members of the COMMD family (Commd1-Commd10) are expressed broadly in many tissues (Burstein et al., 2005; van De Sluis et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: An in-frame deletion in exon 2 of the COMMD1 gene was first identified in Bedlington terrier dogs with hepatic copper toxicosis.
source: An in-frame deletion in exon 2 of the COMMD1 gene was first identified in Bedlington terrier dogs with hepatic copper toxicosis (van De Sluis et al., 2002; Tao et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Commd1 was reported to bind to Cu(II).
source: In accordance with the link of Commd1 to copper metabolism, it was reported to bind to Cu(II), implying that COMMD family members might serve as metal binding proteins (Narindrasorasak et al., 2007), although this was questioned by subsequent studies.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature, but the claim is qualified as being questioned by later studies.

claim: Commd1 has been shown to associate with both ATP7A and ATP7B.
source: Commd1 has also been shown to associate with both ATP7A and ATP7B and is thought to mediate their trafficking from endosomes to the plasma membrane (Materia et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Commd1 is thought to mediate trafficking of ATP7A and ATP7B from endosomes to the plasma membrane.
source: Commd1 has also been shown to associate with both ATP7A and ATP7B and is thought to mediate their trafficking from endosomes to the plasma membrane (Materia et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: ATP7A and ATP7B are responsible for controlling intracellular Cu(II) accumulation in humans.
source: In humans, ATP7A and ATP7B are responsible for controlling intracellular Cu(II) accumulation (Tao et al., 2003; Materia et al., 2012; Vonk et al., 2011; Miyayama et al., 2010; Phillips-Krawczak et al., 2015) and are involved in conditions related to copper toxicity including Wilson's disease (Wang et al., 2011), suggesting an alternative role for Commd1 in copper homeostasis.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ATP7A and ATP7B are involved in conditions related to copper toxicity including Wilson's disease.
source: In humans, ATP7A and ATP7B are responsible for controlling intracellular Cu(II) accumulation (Tao et al., 2003; Materia et al., 2012; Vonk et al., 2011; Miyayama et al., 2010; Phillips-Krawczak et al., 2015) and are involved in conditions related to copper toxicity including Wilson's disease (Wang et al., 2011), suggesting an alternative role for Commd1 in copper homeostasis.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Commd1 depletion causes a marked reduction in surface levels of low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR).
source: In line with a more general function in intracellular trafficking, Commd1 depletion causes a marked reduction in surface levels of low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR), with increased endosomal accumulation leading to a concomitant increase in cholesterol levels (Bartuzi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Commd1 depletion leads to increased endosomal accumulation of LDLR.
source: In line with a more general function in intracellular trafficking, Commd1 depletion causes a marked reduction in surface levels of low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR), with increased endosomal accumulation leading to a concomitant increase in cholesterol levels (Bartuzi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Commd1 depletion leads to a concomitant increase in cholesterol levels.
source: In line with a more general function in intracellular trafficking, Commd1 depletion causes a marked reduction in surface levels of low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR), with increased endosomal accumulation leading to a concomitant increase in cholesterol levels (Bartuzi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Commd9 is deleted in patients with Wilms tumour-aniridia syndrome (WAGR) syndrome.
source: For example, Commd9 is deleted in patients with Wilms tumour-aniridia syndrome (WAGR) syndrome, and appears to interact specifically with Notch2 to regulate its surface abundance by shuttling the receptor away from the lysosomal degradative pathway (Li et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Commd9 appears to interact specifically with Notch2 to regulate its surface abundance.
source: For example, Commd9 is deleted in patients with Wilms tumour-aniridia syndrome (WAGR) syndrome, and appears to interact specifically with Notch2 to regulate its surface abundance by shuttling the receptor away from the lysosomal degradative pathway (Li et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Members of the COMMD family have been linked to nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells (NF-κB) transcriptional regulation.
source: Members of the COMMD family have also been linked to nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells (NF-κB) transcriptional regulation, hypoxia adaptation, and regulation of intracellular sodium concentration via interactions with the epithelial sodium channels (ENaCs) (de Bie et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2013; Maine et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Members of the COMMD family have been linked to hypoxia adaptation.
source: Members of the COMMD family have also been linked to nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells (NF-κB) transcriptional regulation, hypoxia adaptation, and regulation of intracellular sodium concentration via interactions with the epithelial sodium channels (ENaCs) (de Bie et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2013; Maine et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Members of the COMMD family have been linked to regulation of intracellular sodium concentration via interactions with the epithelial sodium channels (ENaCs).
source: Members of the COMMD family have also been linked to nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells (NF-κB) transcriptional regulation, hypoxia adaptation, and regulation of intracellular sodium concentration via interactions with the epithelial sodium channels (ENaCs) (de Bie et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2013; Maine et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: COMMD proteins have been found to exist in an endosome-associated complex with CCDC22 and CCDC93, termed the CCC complex.
source: COMMD proteins have been found to exist in an endosome-associated complex with the coiled-coil domain-containing proteins CCDC22 and CCDC93, which has been termed the CCC (COMMD, CCDC22, CCDC93) complex.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous literature.

claim: The CCC complex can associate with a stable heterotrimeric assembly of VPS29, C16orf62 and DSCR3 to form the Commander or CCC/Retreiver complex.
source: In addition, functional proteomics and bioinformatics have independently shown that the CCC complex can associate with a stable heterotrimeric assembly of VPS29, C16orf62 and DSCR3, to form a larger macromolecular complex dubbed the 'Commander' or CCC/Retreiver complex (Mallam and Marcotte, 2017; Wan et al., 2015; McNally et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SNX17, RanBP1, SH3GLB1 and FAM45a are thought to associate with the Commander complex.
source: Other proteins such as SNX17, RanBP1, SH3GLB1 and FAM45a are also thought to associate with the Commander complex (Wan et al., 2015; Dey et al., 2015; Hein et al., 2015; Huttlin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: COMMD proteins can form homo- and heterodimers through their COMM domains.
source: Further complexity arises from evidence that COMMD proteins can form homo- and heterodimers through their COMM domains (Burstein et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Commd9 and Commd5 associate directly with each other.
source: Although Commd9 and Commd5 associate directly with each other (Wan et al., 2015), it remains unclear whether the COMMD proteins interact physically with each other more generally, or how this relates to their assembly with CCDC22 and CCDC93 in CCC and the larger Commander complex.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Commd1, Commd7 and Commd9 form homodimers and are monodisperse in solution.
source: This showed that Commd1, Commd7 and Commd9 form homodimers and are monodisperse in solution (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by SEC-MALLS data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The Commd1 and Commd9 HN domains behave as monomers.
source: While the Commd1 and Commd9 HN domains behave as monomers, Commd1 and Commd9 COMM domains exist as dimeric species (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by SEC-MALLS data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Commd1 and Commd9 COMM domains exist as dimeric species.
source: While the Commd1 and Commd9 HN domains behave as monomers, Commd1 and Commd9 COMM domains exist as dimeric species (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by SEC-MALLS data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The COMM domain is both required and sufficient to mediate COMMD protein dimerization.
source: This data shows that the COMM domain is both required and sufficient to mediate COMMD protein dimerization.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the SEC-MALLS data showing that isolated COMM domains form dimers while HN domains do not.

claim: The crystal structure of the Commd9 COMM domain was determined to 2.2 Å resolution by single-wavelength anomalous dispersion (SAD).
source: We determined the crystal structure of the Commd9 COMM domain to 2.2 Å resolution by single-wavelength anomalous dispersion (SAD).
evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by the crystallographic data in Table 1.

claim: The overall structure of the Commd9 COMM domain is composed of two cone-shaped chains that are tightly intertwined with each other to form a globular dimeric module.
source: The overall structure of the Commd9 COMM domain is composed of two cone-shaped chains that are tightly intertwined with each other to form a globular dimeric module (Figure 1D, Table 1).
evidence: This is a description of the crystal structure shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Each monomer of the Commd9 COMM domain is comprised of an N-terminal three-stranded β-sheet capped by an α-helix.
source: Each monomer is comprised of an N-terminal three-stranded β-sheet capped by an α-helix, with the overall arrangement making an open, hairpin-like structure.
evidence: This is a description of the crystal structure.

claim: The overlapping C-terminal α-helices of each chain in the Commd9 COMM domain bury a large hydrophobic surface area of approximately 2100 Å2.
source: The overlapping C-terminal α-helices of each chain bury a large hydrophobic surface area of approximately 2100 Å2 (nearly 1/3rd of the monomer surface area) supporting the notion that the native state of COMMD proteins is to form dimers via the COMM domain.
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of the crystal structure.

claim: The buried surface area in the Commd9 COMM domain dimer is nearly 1/3rd of the monomer surface area.
source: The overlapping C-terminal α-helices of each chain bury a large hydrophobic surface area of approximately 2100 Å2 (nearly 1/3rd of the monomer surface area) supporting the notion that the native state of COMMD proteins is to form dimers via the COMM domain.
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of the crystal structure.

claim: There is a very high degree of sequence conservation in the hydrophobic core of the Commd9 COMM domain, particularly along the α-helical surface mediating dimerisation.
source: There is a very high degree of sequence conservation seen in the hydrophobic core of the Commd9 COMM domain, particularly along the α-helical surface mediating dimerisation (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by CONSURF analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Multiple sequence alignment of the COMM domains of all the COMMD proteins demonstrates conservation of many hydrophobic amino acids, particularly leucine residues.
source: Multiple sequence alignment of the COMM domains of all the COMMD proteins demonstrates conservation of many hydrophobic amino acids, particularly leucine residues (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the sequence alignment shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The crystal structure of the Commd9 N-terminal domain was determined to a resolution of 1.55 Å using multi-wavelength anomalous dispersion.
source: We next determined the structure of the Commd9 N-terminal domain by X-ray crystallography to a resolution of 1.55 Å using multi-wavelength anomalous dispersion.
evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by the crystallographic data in Table 1.

claim: The Commd9 N-terminal domain has a globular architecture and is composed of a six-helix bundle with a meander topology.
source: Overall, the Commd9 N-terminal domain has a globular architecture and is composed of a six-helix bundle with a meander topology (Figure 3A, Table 1).
evidence: This is a description of the crystal structure shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The overall structure of the HN domain has a similar all α-helical fold to the equivalent domain of Commd1, which was previously determined by NMR.
source: The overall structure of the HN domain has a similar all α-helical fold to the equivalent domain of Commd1, which was previously determined by NMR (Figure 3B) (Sommerhalter et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a comparison to a previously published structure, supported by citation.

claim: The HN domain of Commd9 has an additional α-helix at its N-terminus compared to Commd1.
source: Compared to Commd1 however, the HN domain of Commd9 has an additional α-helix at its N-terminus that packs down on top of the structure, and a large disordered loop in Commd1 is better resolved in Commd9.
evidence: This is a structural comparison between the Commd9 and Commd1 HN domains.

claim: A large disordered loop in Commd1 is better resolved in Commd9.
source: Compared to Commd1 however, the HN domain of Commd9 has an additional α-helix at its N-terminus that packs down on top of the structure, and a large disordered loop in Commd1 is better resolved in Commd9.
evidence: This is a structural comparison between the Commd9 and Commd1 HN domains.

claim: Comparing the HN domains of Commd1 and Commd9 using DALI showed structural similarity with a DALI Z-score >3.
source: Comparing the HN domains of Commd1 and Commd9 using DALI (Holm and Laakso, 2016; Holm and Rosenström, 2010) showed structural similarity (DALI Z-score >3) with an RMSD of 3.2 Å over 83 Cα atoms.
evidence: This is a quantitative structural comparison using DALI.

claim: The HN domains of Commd1 and Commd9 have an RMSD of 3.2 Å over 83 Cα atoms.
source: Comparing the HN domains of Commd1 and Commd9 using DALI (Holm and Laakso, 2016; Holm and Rosenström, 2010) showed structural similarity (DALI Z-score >3) with an RMSD of 3.2 Å over 83 Cα atoms.
evidence: This is a quantitative structural comparison.

claim: In all of the COMMD family members the HN domain is very likely to share the same α-helical topology.
source: Bioinformatics and secondary structure analyses of the human COMMD proteins however, shows that in all of the family members the HN domain is very likely to share the same α-helical topology, as well as across various species of Commd9 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatics and secondary structure analyses shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The HN domain of human Commd3 shows a strong α–helical signal when examined using far-UV circular dichroism spectroscopy.
source: In support of this, the HN domain of human Commd3 shows a strong α–helical l signal when examined using far-UV circular dichroism spectroscopy (not shown).
evidence: This is experimental data supporting the α-helical nature of the HN domain.

claim: Human Commd6 does not possess an HN domain.
source: The exception to this is human Commd6, which does not possess an HN domain at all, although Commd6 orthologs in other species such as fish and amphibians do (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Commd6 orthologs in other species such as fish and amphibians possess an HN domain.
source: The exception to this is human Commd6, which does not possess an HN domain at all, although Commd6 orthologs in other species such as fish and amphibians do (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The scattering curves and pair distribution functions of Commd1, Commd7 and Commd9 both signify a relatively globular structure.
source: The scattering curves and pair distribution functions (P(r)s) both signify a relatively globular structure.
evidence: This is an interpretation of SAXS data.

claim: Ab initio structures of Commd1, Commd7 and Commd9 calculated from the SAXS data reveal compact but elongated molecules.
source: Ab initio structures of these calculated from the SAXS data reveal compact but elongated molecules.
evidence: This is an interpretation of SAXS data.

claim: The theoretical scattering profiles of Commd1, Commd7 and Commd9 models are in good agreement with the experimental scattering data with low χ2 values.
source: The theoretical scattering profiles of Commd1, Commd7 and Commd9 models, and the ab initio molecular envelopes are in good agreement with the experimental scattering data with low χ2 values.
evidence: This is a validation of the SAXS models against experimental data.

claim: Commd9 is a homodimer with an elongated shape in solution.
source: These studies suggest that the COMMD proteins, including Commd9 are homodimers with an elongated shape in solution.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from SAXS data.

claim: The COMM domain has a similar topology to core fragments of the larger PX and PH structures.
source: Interestingly, it is clear from these comparisons that the COMM domain has a similar topology to core fragments of the larger PX and PH structures (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a structural comparison using DALI.

claim: The COMM domain has structural similarity to the Pur-α repeat domain with a DALI Z-score >4.5.
source: A closer structural match however was identified with the Pur-α (purine-rich element binding protein) repeat domain (DALI Z-score >4.5), a whirly-like nucleic acid binding fold (Graebsch et al., 2009; Weber et al., 2016) (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is a structural comparison using DALI.

claim: Overlay of the Commd9 COMM domain with repeats of Pur-α reveals a similar fold with a RMSD of 2.5 Å over nearly 50 Cα atoms.
source: Overlay of the Commd9 COMM domain with repeats of Pur-α reveals a similar fold with a RMSD of 2.5 Å over nearly 50 Cα atoms.
evidence: This is a quantitative structural comparison.

claim: The clearest structural matches to Commd9 are two closely related proteins from Chlamydia trachomatis (CT584) and Chlamydia pneumoniae (Cpn0803) with DALI Z-scores > 7.5.
source: Intriguingly, the clearest structural matches to Commd9 are two closely related proteins from the bacterial species Chlamydia trachomatis (CT584) and Chlamydia pneumoniae (Cpn0803) (Barta et al., 2013; Stone et al., 2012) (DALI Z-scores > 7.5).
evidence: This is a structural comparison using DALI.

claim: CT584 and Cpn0803 are orthologous proteins found only in chlamydia.
source: CT584 and Cpn0803 are orthologous proteins found only in chlamydia.
evidence: This is a statement about the distribution of these proteins.

claim: CT584 and Cpn0803 are modular proteins with an α-helical N-terminal domain and an α/β C-terminal domain, both of which are structurally analogous to the respective HN and COMM domains of Commd9.
source: They are modular proteins with an α-helical N-terminal domain and an α/β C-terminal domain, both of which are structurally analogous to the respective HN and COMM domains of Commd9 (Figure 4—figure supplement 4B,C).
evidence: This is a structural comparison.

claim: The only major difference in the C-terminal structures between Commd9 and the chlamydial proteins is the presence of two additional α-helices at the C-terminus of the bacterial proteins.
source: The only major difference in the C-terminal structures is the presence of two additional α-helices at the C-terminus of the bacterial proteins (Figure 4—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is a structural comparison.

claim: The N-terminal domains of the chlamydial proteins have an analogous overall topology to the HN domain, except that the bacterial proteins lack α1 and α5.
source: The N-terminal domains of the chlamydial proteins also have an analogous overall topology to the HN domain, except that the bacterial proteins lack α1 and α5 (Figure 4—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This is a structural comparison.

claim: Like the COMMD molecules the chlamydial proteins possess a core dimeric structure formed by the C-terminal domains.
source: Like the COMMD molecules the chlamydial proteins possess a core dimeric structure formed by the C-terminal domains, with an overall architecture that is very similar to that of Commd9 determined by SAXS (Figure 4—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: This is a structural comparison.

claim: Both chlamydial proteins appear to form hexameric assemblies via trimerisation of the core dimer structure.
source: In addition both chlamydial proteins appear to form hexameric assemblies via trimerisation of the core dimer structure (Figure 4—figure supplement 4E) (discussed further below).
evidence: This is based on the crystal structures of the chlamydial proteins.

claim: All of the COMMD proteins are able to co-assemble with each other in a highly promiscuous manner.
source: This assay reveals that all of the COMMD proteins are able to co-assemble with each other in a highly promiscuous manner, while the lack of binding using separately purified proteins suggests that no exchange occurs between pre-formed homodimeric proteins.
evidence: This is supported by co-expression GST pull-down assays shown in Figure 5A.

claim: No exchange occurs between pre-formed homodimeric COMMD proteins.
source: This assay reveals that all of the COMMD proteins are able to co-assemble with each other in a highly promiscuous manner, while the lack of binding using separately purified proteins suggests that no exchange occurs between pre-formed homodimeric proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of binding in pull-down assays using separately purified proteins.

claim: Commd10 binds most strongly to Commd2 and Commd5.
source: In general there is little specificity seen in the heteromeric complexes formed, although Commd10 binds most strongly to Commd2 and Commd5 and only weakly with Commd9, while Commd9 binds weakly to Commd6.
evidence: This is supported by co-expression GST pull-down assays.

claim: Commd10 binds only weakly with Commd9.
source: In general there is little specificity seen in the heteromeric complexes formed, although Commd10 binds most strongly to Commd2 and Commd5 and only weakly with Commd9, while Commd9 binds weakly to Commd6.
evidence: This is supported by co-expression GST pull-down assays.

claim: Commd9 binds weakly to Commd6.
source: In general there is little specificity seen in the heteromeric complexes formed, although Commd10 binds most strongly to Commd2 and Commd5 and only weakly with Commd9, while Commd9 binds weakly to Commd6.
evidence: This is supported by co-expression GST pull-down assays.

claim: The COMM domain alone is sufficient to allow interactions between COMMD proteins.
source: Previous reports have shown that the COMM domain alone may be sufficient to allow interactions between COMMD proteins (Burstein et al., 2005). To test this we next performed our co-expression GST-pull down assays with His-tagged COMM domains of Commd1 and Commd9 and the HN domain of Commd1 as prey. While no interaction was observed between any COMMD proteins and the N-terminal domain of Commd1, strong interactions were seen for C-terminal COMM domains of Commd1 and Commd9 mirroring the full-length proteins (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by co-expression GST pull-down assays shown in Figure 5A and citations to previous literature.

claim: No interaction was observed between any COMMD proteins and the N-terminal domain of Commd1.
source: While no interaction was observed between any COMMD proteins and the N-terminal domain of Commd1, strong interactions were seen for C-terminal COMM domains of Commd1 and Commd9 mirroring the full-length proteins (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by co-expression GST pull-down assays shown in Figure 5A.

claim: COMMD proteins form promiscuous homo- and heterodimeric complexes through their C-terminal COMM domains.
source: Overall, our data indicates that COMMD proteins form promiscuous homo- and heterodimeric complexes through their C-terminal COMM domains.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the co-expression GST pull-down assays.

claim: COMMD-COMMD interactions most likely involve the formation of dimeric structures analogous to that seen in the Commd9 COMM domain crystal structure.
source: The fact that COMMD-COMMD interactions could only be reconstituted after co-translation suggest that these complexes most likely involve the formation of dimeric structures analogous to that seen in the Commd9 COMM domain crystal structure.
evidence: This is an inference based on the requirement for co-translation and the crystal structure.

claim: SEC-MALLS analysis of Commd5-Commd10 reveals that the complex is highly monodisperse in solution.
source: SEC-MALLS analysis of Commd5-Commd10 reveals that the complex is highly monodisperse in solution.
evidence: This is supported by SEC-MALLS data.

claim: The experimental mass of the Commd5-Commd10 complex was calculated to be 85 kDa, suggesting the existence of a Commd5-Commd10 heterotetramer.
source: Although the combined theoretical molecular weight of these proteins is 47.5 kDa, the experimental mass was calculated to be 85 kDa, which suggests the existence of a Commd5-Commd10 heterotetramer (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This is supported by SEC-MALLS data shown in Figure 5E,F.

claim: Commd1, 7 and 10 bind to both CCDC22 and CCDC93 directly.
source: Using the co-translation pull down assay, we found that Commd1, 7 and 10 bind to both CCDC22 and CCDC93 directly (Figure 6A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by co-translation pull-down assays shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Commd9 appears to recognize CCDC93 specifically.
source: Commd9 in contrast appears to recognize CCDC93 specifically.
evidence: This is supported by co-translation pull-down assays.

claim: CCDC22 and CCDC93 bind to COMMDs chiefly through the NN-CH domain.
source: We next performed domain-truncations and conducted the binding assay with isolated calponin homology-like domains (NN-CH) and C-terminal coiled coil regions of CCDC22 and CCDC93. Interestingly, CCDC22 and CCDC93 bind to COMMDs chiefly through the NN-CH domain.
evidence: This is supported by domain truncation pull-down assays.

claim: COMMD-CCDC22/CCDC93 binding occurs through the COMM domain.
source: Our data also shows that similar to COMMD-COMMD interaction, COMMD-CCDC22/CCDC93 binding occurs through the COMM domain.
evidence: This is supported by domain truncation pull-down assays.

claim: CCDC22 and CCDC93 interaction with pre-formed COMMD dimers occurs spontaneously in vitro.
source: In contrast to interactions between COMMD family members, which require co-expression for assembly, we find that CCDC22 and CCDC93 interaction with pre-formed COMMD dimers occurs spontaneously in vitro (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by GST pull-down experiments with purified proteins shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Commd1 and Commd9 bind more strongly to the N-terminal NN-CH domain of CCDC93 in comparison to CCDC22.
source: Specifically, Commd1 and Commd9 bind more strongly to the N-terminal NN-CH domain of CCDC93 in comparison to CCDC22.
evidence: This is supported by GST pull-down experiments.

claim: Commd1 has stronger affinity than Commd9 for CCDC proteins.
source: Moreover, this assay also suggests that Commd1 has stronger affinity than Commd9 for CCDC proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from GST pull-down experiments.

claim: The affinity (Kd) of the COMM domain of Commd1 with NN-CH of CCDC22 was calculated to be 10.3 µM.
source: A dose-dependent increase in the binding of the COMM domain of Commd1 with NN-CH of CCDC22 and CCDC93 was observed, and the affinity (Kd) was calculated to be 10.3 and 14.6 µM respectively (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is supported by biolayer interferometry data shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: The affinity (Kd) of the COMM domain of Commd1 with NN-CH of CCDC93 was calculated to be 14.6 µM.
source: A dose-dependent increase in the binding of the COMM domain of Commd1 with NN-CH of CCDC22 and CCDC93 was observed, and the affinity (Kd) was calculated to be 10.3 and 14.6 µM respectively (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is supported by biolayer interferometry data shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: Cross-linking mass spectrometry revealed 3 unique cross-links connecting Commd9 and NN-CH domain of CCDC93.
source: Analyses of MS data from band 2 revealed 5 unique cross-links, and 3 of these pairs connected Commd9 and NN-CH domain of CCDC93 (Figure 7B and Table 3).
evidence: This is supported by cross-linking mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 7B and Table 3.

claim: All three lysines (K100, K133 and K152) that cross-linked to CCDC93 were located on the surface accessible to the solvent in Commd9.
source: Mapping of these pairs onto the crystal structures of Commd9 showed that all three lysines (K100, K133 and K152) were located on the surface accessible to the solvent (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This is supported by mapping cross-links onto the crystal structure shown in Figure 7C,D.

claim: K133 and K152 are located on contiguous surfaces of the β-sheets of the COMM domains, suggesting a likely binding surface for the CCDC93 NN-CH domain.
source: Notably, K133 and K152 are located on contiguous surfaces of the β-sheets of the COMM domains (Figure 7D), suggesting a likely binding surface for the CCDC93 NN-CH domain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the location of cross-linked residues shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The likely binding surface for CCDC93 on the COMM domain includes the side-chains of the conserved residues 128WRVD131, with Trp128 being strictly conserved across the entire Commd family.
source: This surface also includes the side-chains of the conserved residues 128WRVD131, with Trp128 in particular being strictly conserved across the entire Commd family (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis and sequence conservation shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Commd1 associates relatively non-specifically with various negatively charged membranes.
source: The assay shows that Commd1 associates relatively non-specifically with various negatively charged membranes, including PC/PE liposomes doped with different phosphoinositides, generic Folch lipids from brain extracts, and liposomes containing 30% phosphatidylinositolserine (PS).
evidence: This is supported by liposome-pelleting assays shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Commd7 shows similar binding characteristics to Commd1 for negatively charged membranes.
source: We observed a similar binding characteristic for Commd7, but Commd10 showed a relatively strong interaction with Folch liposomes as well as di- and tri- phosphorylated phosphoinositide species.
evidence: This is supported by liposome-pelleting assays.

claim: Commd10 showed a relatively strong interaction with Folch liposomes as well as di- and tri- phosphorylated phosphoinositide species.
source: We observed a similar binding characteristic for Commd7, but Commd10 showed a relatively strong interaction with Folch liposomes as well as di- and tri- phosphorylated phosphoinositide species.
evidence: This is supported by liposome-pelleting assays.

claim: Commd9 appears to associate weakly if at all with the membranes tested.
source: In contrast to the other family members, Commd9 appears to associate weakly if at all with the membranes tested (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by liposome-pelleting assays shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The Commd1 COMM domain exhibits a basic patch on its surface composed of solvent-exposed positively charged residues that are absent in Commd9.
source: A comparative analysis of the electrostatic surface of the COMM domain of Commd9 and a homology model of the COMM domain of Commd1 (constructed using the COMM domain of Commd9 as the template) shows that the Commd1 COMM domain exhibits a basic patch on its surface composed of solvent-exposed positively charged residues that are absent in Commd9 (Figure 8B,C).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 8B,C.

claim: The Commd1 triple mutant (R133Q, H134A and K167A) shows a drastic reduction in membrane interaction.
source: To test if this basic surface on Commd1 is involved in membrane recruitment, we made a triple mutant in the putative lipid-binding site (R133Q, H134A and K167A). In liposome-pelleting assays this mutant shows a drastic reduction in membrane interaction (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by liposome-pelleting assays shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Commd1 possesses a higher level of binding response for phosphoinositides PI(3)P and PI(4,5)P2 compared to Folch and PS containing membranes.
source: While Commd1 possesses a higher level of binding response for phosphoinositides PI(3)P and PI(4,5)P2 compared to Folch and PS containing membranes, Commd9 showed little association with any of the lipids tested, in line with the liposome-pelleting assay (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by BLiTz data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: Commd9 showed little association with any of the lipids tested.
source: While Commd1 possesses a higher level of binding response for phosphoinositides PI(3)P and PI(4,5)P2 compared to Folch and PS containing membranes, Commd9 showed little association with any of the lipids tested, in line with the liposome-pelleting assay (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by BLiTz data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: Commd1 binds to a variety of liposomes with similar affinities in the range of 1–10 µM.
source: Commd1 binds to a variety of liposomes with similar affinities in the range of 1–10 µM, which is in agreement with the qualitative results from pelleting assays (Figure 8D,E,F,G and H).
evidence: This is supported by BLiTz data shown in Figure 8D-H.

claim: No interaction was observed between liposomes and the Commd1 triple mutant.
source: Confirming the importance of the basic patch on the Commd1 COMM domain, no interaction was observed with the Commd1 triple mutant.
evidence: This is supported by BLiTz data.

claim: The COMM domain of COMMD proteins appears to be a central hub for both protein-protein and protein-membrane interactions.
source: Altogether, the COMM domain of COMMD proteins appears to be a central hub for both protein-protein and protein-membrane interactions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence including binding assays and structural data.

claim: GFP-tagged Commd1 wild type is localized to endosomal puncta and colocalises with the WASH complex subunit Fam21.
source: As seen previously, Commd1 is localized to endosomal puncta, and colocalises with the WASH complex subunit Fam21.
evidence: This is supported by confocal immunofluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 8I.

claim: The mutant Commd1 (R133Q, H134A, K167A) is also colocalised with Fam21 on endosomes, despite being defective for membrane binding in vitro.
source: Surprisingly however, the mutant Commd1 is also colocalised with Fam21 on endosomes, despite being defective for membrane binding in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by confocal immunofluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 8I.

claim: The membrane-binding site on Commd1 may be important for non-specific membrane interactions and perhaps for the orientation of the CCC complex on endosomes, but is not required for specific recruitment to PtdIns3P-enriched endosomal compartments in the context of the assembled complex.
source: We propose therefore that this site on Commd1 may instead be important for non-specific membrane interactions and perhaps for the orientation of the CCC complex on endosomes, but in the context of the assembled complex with other COMMD proteins it is not required for specific recruitment to PtdIns3P-enriched endosomal compartments.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the observation that the mutant Commd1 still localizes to endosomes.

claim: The CCC complex is a large endosome-associated assembly that regulates cell surface recycling of various transmembrane receptors.
source: The COMMD proteins were recently identified as conserved and central components of the CCC complex (Mallam and Marcotte, 2017; Wan et al., 2015; McNally et al., 2017), a large endosome-associated assembly that regulates cell surface recycling of various transmembrane receptors (McNally et al., 2017; Phillips-Krawczak et al., 2015; Bartuzi et al., 2016; Wan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The solution structures of Commd1, Commd7 and Commd9 reveal a modular architecture with the α-helical N-terminal HN domains arranged as flexible appendages to the C-terminal COMM domain dimers.
source: The solution structures of Commd1, Commd7 and Commd9 reveal a modular architecture with the α-helical N-terminal HN domains arranged as flexible appendages to the C-terminal COMM domain dimers.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from SAXS data.

claim: The HN domain is a structurally conserved feature shared by all COMMD family members.
source: Our biophysical, structural and bioinformatics analyses however show that the HN domain is a structurally conserved feature shared by all COMMD family members.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from structural and bioinformatics analyses.

claim: The architecture of the COMMD proteins bears a remarkable resemblance to the orthologous CT584 and Cpn0803, Chlamydia-specific proteins from C. trachomatis and C. pneumonia respectively.
source: The architecture of the COMMD proteins revealed here bears a remarkable resemblance to the orthologous CT584 and Cpn0803, Chlamydia-specific proteins from C. trachomatis and C. pneumonia respectively.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from structural comparisons.

claim: There is evidence that Cpn0803 can interact with phospholipids as well as components of the Type III secretion system.
source: The function of these proteins is unknown, although there is evidence that Cpn0803 can interact with phospholipids as well as components of the Type III secretion system responsible for injection of bacterial effectors into the host cytoplasm (Stone et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The CT584/Cpn0803 proteins may be secreted effectors with a potential to mimic or modify COMMD protein functions.
source: We speculate therefore that the CT584/Cpn0803 proteins may be secreted effectors with a potential to mimic or modify COMMD protein functions, although this remains to be confirmed.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the structural similarity and known properties of chlamydial effectors.

claim: Several chlamydial proteins are believed to have evolved through horizontal gene transfer from eukaryotic hosts.
source: Several chlamydial proteins are believed to have evolved through horizontal gene transfer from eukaryotic hosts, such as SWIB domain-containing proteins and Swi/Snf2 helicases (Bastidas and Valdivia, 2016; Stephens et al., 1998), and it is possible that the CT584/Cpn0803 genes have been acquired in a similar fashion.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and is a speculation about the evolutionary origin of CT584/Cpn0803.

claim: Both CT584 and Cpn0803 form hexameric structures composed of a trimer of dimers, with the N-terminal domains providing the primary interface for trimer formation.
source: Both CT584 and Cpn0803 form hexameric structures composed of a trimer of dimers, with the N-terminal domains providing the primary interface for trimer formation (Barta et al., 2013; Stone et al., 2012) (Figure 4—figure supplement 4E).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4E.

claim: The N-terminal domains of COMMD proteins may contribute to formation of higher-order heteromeric assemblies that are present in the 600 kDa CCC complexes isolated from cultured cells.
source: While full-length recombinant Commd1, Commd7 and Commd9 proteins analysed here form homodimers, it is tempting to speculate that the N-terminal domains of COMMD proteins will contribute to formation of higher-order heteromeric assemblies that are present in the 600 kDa CCC complexes isolated from cultured cells (Wan et al., 2015), the stoichiometries and structures of which remain to be determined.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the structural similarity to chlamydial proteins and the known size of CCC complexes.

claim: Commd1 has been shown to be a potent inhibitor of the transcription factor NF-κB.
source: Most prominently, Commd1 has been shown to be a potent inhibitor of the transcription factor NF-κB, a master regulator of inflammation, and other COMMD proteins also display similar activities (Maine and Burstein, 2007; de Bie et al., 2006; Ganesh et al., 2003; Bartuzi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Other COMMD proteins also display similar activities to Commd1 in inhibiting NF-κB.
source: Most prominently, Commd1 has been shown to be a potent inhibitor of the transcription factor NF-κB, a master regulator of inflammation, and other COMMD proteins also display similar activities (Maine and Burstein, 2007; de Bie et al., 2006; Ganesh et al., 2003; Bartuzi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Commd1 acts downstream of the inhibitory IκB kinase.
source: Commd1 acts downstream of the inhibitory IκB kinase (Ganesh et al., 2003), and is believed to associate with NF-κB subunits at chromosomal loci and promote NF-κB ubiquitination by Cullin family ubiquitin ligases for degradation (Maine et al., 2007; Mao et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Commd1 is believed to associate with NF-κB subunits at chromosomal loci and promote NF-κB ubiquitination by Cullin family ubiquitin ligases for degradation.
source: Commd1 acts downstream of the inhibitory IκB kinase (Ganesh et al., 2003), and is believed to associate with NF-κB subunits at chromosomal loci and promote NF-κB ubiquitination by Cullin family ubiquitin ligases for degradation (Maine et al., 2007; Mao et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A similar function has been proposed for Commd1 regulation of the HIF-1α transcription factor.
source: A similar function has been proposed for Commd1 regulation of the HIF-1α transcription factor (van de Sluis et al., 2007, 2010, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The COMM domain fold is structurally related to the repeat domains found in the PUR family protein Pur-α.
source: The COMM domain fold is structurally related to the repeat domains found in the PUR (purine-rich element binding protein) family protein Pur-α (Graebsch et al., 2009; Weber et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparisons and citations to previous literature.

claim: Pur-α contains three repeat domains, the first two of which form an intramolecular 'dimer' while the third forms an intermolecular dimer that both resemble the dimeric COMM domain topology.
source: Pur-α contains three such repeat domains, the first two of which form an intramolecular 'dimer' while the third forms an intermolecular dimer (Weber et al., 2016) that both resemble the dimeric COMM domain topology.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Pur-α is a nucleic acid binding protein that plays important roles in the transcription of neuronal genes.
source: Pur-α is a nucleic acid binding protein that plays important roles in the transcription of neuronal genes (Gallia et al., 2000; White et al., 2009), and is associated with GGGGCC-containing inclusions in ALS-FTD patients (Xu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Pur-α is associated with GGGGCC-containing inclusions in ALS-FTD patients.
source: Pur-α is a nucleic acid binding protein that plays important roles in the transcription of neuronal genes (Gallia et al., 2000; White et al., 2009), and is associated with GGGGCC-containing inclusions in ALS-FTD patients (Xu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The similarity of the COMM domain with Pur-α suggests the intriguing possibility that COMMD proteins could also interact with DNA and/or RNA to regulate transcription.
source: The similarity of the COMM domain with Pur-α suggests the intriguing possibility that COMMD proteins could also interact with DNA and/or RNA to regulate transcription, although it should be noted that the specific DNA binding site in Pur-α (Weber et al., 2016) is not conserved in the COMMD proteins (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is a speculation based on structural similarity, but qualified by the lack of conservation of the DNA binding site.

claim: The specific DNA binding site in Pur-α is not conserved in the COMMD proteins.
source: The similarity of the COMM domain with Pur-α suggests the intriguing possibility that COMMD proteins could also interact with DNA and/or RNA to regulate transcription, although it should be noted that the specific DNA binding site in Pur-α (Weber et al., 2016) is not conserved in the COMMD proteins (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The CCC complex and associated COMMD proteins are predominantly localised to early endosomal membranes.
source: The CCC complex and associated COMMD proteins are predominantly localised to early endosomal membranes (Phillips-Krawczak et al., 2015; Bartuzi et al., 2016; Wan et al., 2015; McNally et al., 2017; Burkhead et al., 2009; Drévillon et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The HN domain is dispensable for membrane association of COMMD proteins.
source: Our data also highlights that the HN domain is dispensable for membrane association, which is in line with the work of Burkhead et al. (Burkhead et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and a citation to previous literature.

claim: The membrane-binding surface of Commd1 in vitro is composed of residues from both molecules of the homodimer.
source: The membrane-binding surface of Commd1 in vitro is composed of residues from both molecules of the homodimer, but interestingly this does not appear essential for endosomal localisation of Commd1 in cells.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis and mutagenesis data.

claim: The ability of COMMD proteins to associate with membranes is only one part of a more complicated array of interactions controlling specific endosomal membrane recruitment.
source: This suggests that the ability of COMMD proteins to associate with membranes is only one part of a more complicated array of interactions controlling specific endosomal membrane recruitment, likely involving different lipid binding properties of heterodimeric COMMD proteins and other CCC complex subunits.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that the membrane-binding mutant still localizes to endosomes.

claim: The depletion of CCDC93 or the WASH complex subunit Fam21 both lead to a loss of Commd1 from endosomes.
source: Supporting a role for other subunits and complexes in specific endosomal localisation of the CCC complex, the depletion of CCDC93 or the WASH complex subunit Fam21 both lead to a loss of Commd1 from endosomes (Phillips-Krawczak et al., 2015), while the depletion of CCDC22 causes a redistribution of Commd1 and Commd10 (Starokadomskyy et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The depletion of CCDC22 causes a redistribution of Commd1 and Commd10.
source: Supporting a role for other subunits and complexes in specific endosomal localisation of the CCC complex, the depletion of CCDC93 or the WASH complex subunit Fam21 both lead to a loss of Commd1 from endosomes (Phillips-Krawczak et al., 2015), while the depletion of CCDC22 causes a redistribution of Commd1 and Commd10 (Starokadomskyy et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The ability to self-assemble and form heteromeric complexes is a core property of the COMMD proteins.
source: The ability to self-assemble and form heteromeric complexes is a core property of the COMMD proteins identified in some of the very first studies (Burstein et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Coordinates and structure factors for the COMM and HN domain of Commd9 have been deposited at the Protein Data Bank (PDB) with accession codes 6BP6 (COMM domain Commd9) and 4OE9 (HN domain of Commd9).
source: Coordinates and structure factors for the COMM and HN domain of Commd9 have been deposited at the Protein Data Bank (PDB) with accession codes 6BP6 (COMM domain Commd9) and 4OE9 (HN domain of Commd9).
evidence: This is a data availability statement.
